name: Szczerbiec
powers: Symbol of Polish kingship; the notched blade carries the Kiev legend.
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged coronation sword of the kings of Poland, is the only surviving piece of the medieval Polish crown jewels and is kept in the treasure vault of Wawel Castle in Kraków. Its name comes from the Polish szczerba, 'gap' or 'notch', and legend attributes the damage to Bolesław the Brave, said to have struck the blade against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018, though the gate was not built until 1037 and the surviving sword dates to the thirteenth century. The hilt is decorated with Christian symbols, floral ornament and magical formulae, and a narrow slit in the blade holds a small shield bearing the Polish coat of arms. The earliest known use of the name is in the Chronicle of Greater Poland, which records an angel giving the sword to Bolesław so that he would triumph in battle. First used at a coronation in 1320, the sword was looted by Prussian troops in 1795, passed through nineteenth-century collections, and was returned to Poland only in the twentieth century after being evacuated during the Second World War. The legend of the notched blade remains a powerful emblem of Polish kingship and national memory.
source: Wawel Crown Jewels; coronation tradition

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, the Svatováclavská koruna, was made in 1347 for the coronation of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, and was named after the tenth-century Bohemian duke and martyr Saint Wenceslas. It is set with large rubies, sapphires, emeralds, spinels and pearls, and together with the orb, sceptre and coronation robes it forms the Bohemian crown jewels, now kept in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. The crown carries a famous curse: legend holds that a usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year, a fate sometimes connected with the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich, though the story is modern and unverifiable. Because of the legend the crown is shown rarely, displayed only on high feast days and under strict conditions, with seven keys held by separate officials. The medieval form, with its pointed arches and jewel-encrusted circlet, makes it one of the most striking royal insignia in Europe.
source: Bohemian crown jewels; Prague legend

name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is the hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a bearded figure in pointed Tatar dress and Mongol robes who parades the Old Town each year on the first Thursday after Corpus Christi, playfully striking onlookers with his gilded wooden mace to bring them good luck. Legend traces the custom to 1287, when Vistula raftsmen of the Zwierzyniec district, called włóczkowie, are said to have surprised and overwhelmed a sleeping Tatar raiding party camped by the river, then ridden into the city dressed in the captives' robes to celebrate their victory. The earliest written notices of the procession date from the 1730s and 1750s, and the mayor still greets the Lajkonik at the Main Market Square with a ceremonial ransom of money and a toast drunk from a chalice. The key elements of its costume, from the cream-crested head to the golden mace, were designed in 1909 by Stanisław Wyspiański, and the figure remains one of the unofficial symbols of Kraków, reproduced on trams, shop signs and festival posters.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Poland, distinguished by a square crown whose corners fold out over the rim, evolved from the konfederatka worn by the Confederates of Bar in 1768-1772. Under the Second Polish Republic it became the standard headgear of the Polish Army, worn in khaki and grey by infantry and in crimson by the mounted uhlans, and variants served Polish units through the Second World War and into the modern armed forces. The four corners are traditionally said to mark the four quarters of the world or the soldier's virtues, and the cap also became a piece of civil national dress, still worn with folk costume, on ceremonial occasions and by marching bands. Because of its insurrection and wartime associations the rogatywka carries a heavy symbolic charge as a badge of Polish independence, and modern reproductions are made by military tailors for parades, re-enactments and formal dress.
source: Histories of Polish military dress

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is the Polish folk art of paper cutting, practised above all by village women from the nineteenth century, who folded and snipped dyed paper with heavy sheep shears to make flat wall decorations. Regional schools differ sharply: the celebrated cutouts of Łowicz build up layers of brightly coloured paper into leafy bouquets, rosettes and birds, while Kurpie makers favour single-colour, symmetrical designs such as the jedynak, cut from one folded sheet in black, red or gold. The cutouts were pasted on the whitewashed beams and walls of rural cottages, hung around holy pictures and given as wedding gifts, borrowing their motifs freely from embroidery, tile painting and woven bands. Though few farmhouses now display them in the old way, wycinanki survive as an emblem of Polish folk identity, taught in workshops and collected in ethnographic museums such as those at Łowicz and Warsaw.
source: Studies of Polish folk paper-cutting

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a Nativity crib built as a glittering model of the city itself, cramming Wawel Cathedral, St Mary's Basilica, castle towers, spires and arcades into a many-storeyed facade of cardboard, tin foil and painted paper around the central stable. The tradition took shape in the nineteenth century, when Kraków bricklayers and building workers made portable cribs to earn money at Christmas, and it gained its civic form after 1937, when the first official contest was held; makers known as krakowianie still compete every first Thursday of December on the Main Market Square beside the Adam Mickiewicz monument. The best szopki show great technical ambition, with moving figures, hidden candle-lit interiors and window scenes re-enacting nativity and patriotic tableaux. In 2018 UNESCO inscribed the szopka tradition on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and collections such as the one in the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków preserve competition winners going back decades.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of fresh willow twigs that Czech boys carry on Easter Monday, when they go from house to house lightly switching girls and women to wish them health, freshness and beauty, receiving painted eggs and coloured ribbons in return. The name comes from pomladit, 'to make young again', and the custom preserves an old spring-renewal rite of driving out winter and coaxing new life, in which the willow, one of the first trees to bud, was held to carry special power. Skilled makers plait eight, twelve or even more rods into a smooth handle, bind the tip with ribbon and often add a pair of dangling tassels, weaving the whip anew each spring. In Moravia the same whip is called the šibačka and in Slovakia the korbáč, and after the morning round the girls may pour water or perfume over the boys in the related Easter-Monday wetting custom.
source: Czech and Slovak ethnography of Easter customs

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted baubles made in the glass towns of northern Bohemia, above all around Jablonec nad Nisou and the Krkonoše foothills, where the craft grew out of the region's bead and glass-button industry in the mid-nineteenth century. Workers blew thin globes from molten glass, silvered them from inside with a solution that gave the characteristic metallic glimmer, and then painted them by hand with snow, berries, flowers or fairy-tale figures before hanging them from the family fir tree. The delicate ornaments became a celebrated export, so prized that Bohemian and Moravian glassmakers supplied Christmas trees across Europe and America for more than a century. A few family workshops still fire the baubles by mouth today, and the region's museums display both the finished ornaments and the wooden and metal tools of the old glasshuts.
source: Histories of Bohemian glassmaking

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a very long overtone flute of the Slovak shepherds, the central instrument of the Podpoľanie region, made from elder, maple or ash wood and reaching 160 to 200 centimetres in length, with a short side tube that carries the wind to the main bore. It has only three finger holes, yet a skilled player produces a low, humming bass and high, crying overtones by overblowing, and the traditional repertoire imitates the gurgle of springs, the wind and long pastoral calls. Shepherds played the fujara while tending flocks on the slopes of Poľana, and each maker decorated the instrument individually with burnt or carved ornament, so no two fujaras are alike. UNESCO proclaimed the fujara and its music a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008, and it is now heard both at folk festivals in Detva and in concert music.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotarstvo is the Slovak craft of working iron wire, born in the eighteenth century when travelling drotári from the hills of northern Slovakia walked across Europe mending cracked pottery, glass and pipes with fine wire bindings. What began as tinkering became an art: journeymen and masters built up latticework jugs, birdcages, vases and small household utensils entirely from wire, and the reinforced pots with their neat braided seams were admired as folk masterpieces. The craft was carried by emigrant drotári as far as Russia, the Balkans and America, and the region around Považie in particular produced dynasties of wiremen. In 2019 UNESCO inscribed drotarstvo on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and museums in Bratislava and Považská Bystrica preserve both the tools and the elaborate wirework that survives from the trade's heyday.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnography

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small axe of the Carpathian shepherds, a light iron head set on a long wooden haft that reaches the waist, serving at once as walking staff, digging tool and weapon. Slovak bača shepherds and hikers of the High Tatras carry the valaška through the mountains, and its handle is often ornamented with engraved patterns or metal mountings that mark the maker and the owner. Folk legend places the valaška in the hand of Juraj Jánošík, the eighteenth-century outlaw of the Tatra country who is said to have robbed the nobles and shared the booty with the poor, and the axe became an attribute of highland identity as much as the flute and the pipe. In the twentieth century the valaška was adopted as an emblem of Slovak mountaineering and folk life, and carved examples are kept as souvenirs and in ethnographic collections.
material: forged iron blade, carved wood handle
source: Slovak folklore and highland ethnography

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is the Bulgarian talisman of March, a twisted length of red and white yarn, often finished with beads or a small tassel, exchanged on 1 March to wish health, strength and good fortune for the new year. The red stands for life and the blood, the white for purity and spring light, and the name honours Baba Marta, the capricious old woman of folk belief whose moods are said to govern the early-spring weather. The martenitsa is worn on the wrist, lapel or neck until the wearer sees a stork, a swallow or the first blossoming tree, then it is tied to a fruit tree so the tree will bear, or slipped under a stone for luck. The custom, shared across Bulgaria and its neighbours, was inscribed in 2017 on the UNESCO Representative List through a joint file on 1 March cultural practices, and whole streets of Bulgaria are strung with martenitsi every spring.
source: Bulgarian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are the masked dancers of the Bulgarian winter, men dressed from head to foot in sheepskin and goat-hide, crowned with tall carved wooden masks and hung about the waist with heavy bronze and copper bells, who process through villages around New Year and before Lent. Their dance - a hopping, swaying, bell-shaking performance - is meant to drive out evil spirits, ill luck and sickness and to bring health, fertility and a good harvest in the season to come. Masks differ from region to region: Pernik favours towering feathered and horned figures, while the Rhodope makers carve flatter, beast-like faces, and each costume can weigh tens of kilograms. Since 1966 the International Festival of Masquerade Games Surva in Pernik has gathered hundreds of groups every January, and in 2015 UNESCO inscribed the Surova folk feast of the Pernik region on the Representative List.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, an instrument built from a whole tanned goatskin that serves as the air bag, with a chanter pipe for the melody and a single long drone pipe that sounds a constant bass note. Its bright, cutting tone comes from a single beating reed in the chanter, and a skilled player holds the bag under the arm, fingers the chanter's holes and taps out rhythms as he squeezes. The gaida is the leading instrument of Bulgarian folk music, accompanying the horo line dances at weddings, village feasts and festivals, and in the Rodopi mountains it is traditionally played for the slow, meandering dance tunes of the region. Because shepherds were the first players, the gaida is bound up with the pastoral life, and it remains the national instrument of Bulgaria, heard from folk ensembles to wedding bands.
source: Bulgarian ethnomusicology

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the traditional Serbian cap, a rounded woollen cap with a raised crown whose four points fold into a characteristic V shape, made from a single piece of cloth and worn without a visor. Its name honours the šajkaši, the eighteenth-century Serbian river troops who crewed the šajka boats of the Danube and Sava under Habsburg command and who first wore the shape. From the nineteenth century the šajkača spread beyond the river garrisons to Serbian soldiers, teachers, priests and peasants, becoming a badge of Serbian national identity, worn in the Balkan Wars and the First World War and banned by the occupiers during the Second. The V of the crown is sometimes read as the spread wings of the eagle, and today the cap is worn at ceremonies, in folk ensembles and by diaspora Serbs as a mark of origin and belonging.
source: Histories of Serbian military dress and ethnography

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, built on a vertical loom with a cotton warp and a dense woollen weft that produces a flat, reversible fabric. Weavers worked in the so-called vratilnice technique, knotting and braiding the weft in long strips so that the patterns interlock, and the classical designs pair a central medallion with borders of zigzags, hooks and stylised flowers in red, black, white and green. In the nineteenth century Pirot rugs hung on walls, covered floors and chests and formed part of the bride's dowry, and the town's weavers supplied households across the Balkans and the Ottoman court. Woven by women who guarded the pattern-books on the same looms, the Pirot kilim is counted a Serbian national symbol, and a small circle of masters still weaves it today.
source: Serbian textile and craft studies

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is the traditional leather shoe of the Serbian countryside, a soft moccasin cut from a single piece of cured pig or calf hide, stitched at the heel and gathered over the foot with thongs that cross above the ankle. Its most striking feature is the turned-up toe, the špic, which lifted the foot clear of dew, grass and stones and, in the most famous regional pattern, curls back into a small horn over the instep. Opanci were worn with woollen footcloths called obojci and tied with long straps, and they served peasants, herdsmen and even soldiers for centuries before factory footwear displaced them. Because almost every village had its own cut - the wide Šumadija form, the sharp Bosnian toe, the flat Montenegrin sole - the opanak became a strong marker of Serbian folk dress and is still worn at festivals, by folk dancers and on ceremonial occasions.
source: Serbian folk dress studies

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, built up from a ground shell core coated with layer after layer of a milky emulsion made from the scales of the plasica, a small silvery fish endemic to Lake Ohrid. Because the recipe and the painstaking process are guarded as family secrets, only two families - the Talevs, who bought the formula in 1924, and the Filevs, who learned it in 1928 - have made authentic Ohrid pearls, passing the craft from father to son and hand-coating each grain up to ten times. Local tradition credits the secret to Jovan Subanović, a Russian emigrant said to have brought the technique to Ohrid after the 1917 revolution, and the name 'Ohrid Pearl' was fixed by 1935. Their soft lustre and durability made them famous beyond the Balkans; Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana are said to have worn them, and a handmade necklace remains a proud family heirloom.
source: Macedonian craft and jewellery studies

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a double flute of North Macedonia, carved from a single piece of wood, sometimes elder or ash, as two parallel pipes joined at the mouth, with fingerholes on one pipe only. The second, unholed pipe serves as a drone, sounding a steady note beneath the melody and giving the instrument its haunting, reedy character; regional names include dvojnica, and similar double flutes are known across the Balkans. Shepherds played the dvojanka in the mountains, and it accompanied the slow, ornamented tunes of Macedonian pastoral music, the whistle of the drone carrying over pasture and dance ground alike. A small community of folk musicians and instrument makers keeps the dvojanka alive today, and it is heard at ethnographic concerts and village festivals alongside the kaval and the gaida.
source: Macedonian ethnomusicology

name: Koschei's Needle
description: Needle in which the Russian fairy-tale villain Koschei the Deathless hides his soul, so that he cannot be killed while it remains intact. In Afanasyev's collected tales the needle lies inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a hare, and the hare inside a chest locked on an island oak; the hero must open each container in turn and break the needle to destroy Koschei. The motif recurs across Slavic and wider folklore, and variants replace the needle with a flower, a spider or a bird's egg. Folklorists class it among the 'external soul' tales, in which a being stores its life force outside its body for safety; the moment the chain of containers is broken, the villain collapses and dies. The needle is therefore the hinge of the whole story, and the hero's task becomes one of patience and sequence rather than of strength.
material: iron needle (in the tale, nested in egg, duck, hare, chest)
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Koschei the Deathless)

name: Baba Yaga's Mortar and Pestle
description: Iron mortar and pestle ridden by Baba Yaga, the witch of Russian fairy tales, who flies over the forest in her mortar, sweeping away her trail with a broom and driving the mortar onward with the pestle. In Afanasyev's tales she is called 'Baba Yaga the Bone Leg' and travels in this way; the mortar, pestle and broom are among the most iconic props of Russian folk narrative. Folklorists note that the mortar echoes the work of grain-pounding and the boundary between the farmstead and the wild, fitting the witch who lives at the edge of the forest. She is sometimes said to fly at great speed, using the pestle as her engine and the broom to erase her traces so that pursuers cannot follow. The trio of mortar, pestle and broom has passed into art, film and illustration wherever Baba Yaga appears, and remains instantly recognisable even outside Slavic tradition.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' (Baba Yaga tales)

name: Firebird's Feather
description: Golden feather of the Firebird (Zhar-ptitsa) of Russian fairy tales, which shines so brightly that it lights a whole dark room and is carried by heroes such as Ivan Tsarevich into the tsar's palace. In Afanasyev's tale the feather, and later the bird itself, is sought as a task set by the tsar; the radiant Firebird became a favourite motif of Russian decorative art. The feather is usually the first test: the hero who takes it must then capture the living bird, often with a golden cage, and afterwards the horse with the golden mane and the fair princess Vasilisa. Because the bird is otherworldly, its feather is sometimes said to burn whatever it touches and to heal the sick if kept near. The motif later inspired Stravinsky's 1910 ballet 'The Firebird', which made the glowing feather a worldwide image of Russian fairy-tale art.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('The Firebird')

name: Vasilisa's Doll
description: Small wooden doll given to Vasilisa by her dying mother in the Russian fairy tale, which eats a morsel of the girl's food and helps her perform impossible tasks so that she survives her cruel stepmother and Baba Yaga. Recorded in Afanasyev's collection as 'Vasilisa the Beautiful', the doll is the helper-object of the tale, a folk counterpart to the magical helpers of later European fairy tales. The mother's blessing is essential: the doll works only for Vasilisa, must be fed a little food, and loses its power if others discover it. When Baba Yaga sets the impossible tasks of sorting grain, cleaning the hut and weaving cloth, the doll completes them overnight, and the witch herself wonders how the girl succeeds. The doll is sometimes said to carry the soul of the dead mother watching over her daughter; folklorists read it as motherly care transformed into a protective object.
source: Afanasyev, 'Russian Fairy Tales' ('Vasilisa the Beautiful')

name: Gusli (Russian Psaltery)
description: Ancient Russian plucked zither, a shallow trapezoid or helmet-shaped board with gut or metal strings, played by the epic singers who performed the byliny. The legendary Novgorod merchant Sadko of the byliny plays the gusli so well that the Sea Tsar summons him to the underwater palace; the instrument is attested in chronicles, miniatures and archaeological finds from Novgorod. Excavated Novgorod gusli date from the 11th to the 14th centuries and were carved from a single block of wood, often with a decorated sound hole. In the bylina Sadko's playing so delights the Sea Tsar that the hero is offered a bride among the sea maidens, and when the gusli breaks the music stops and the underwater court falls silent. The instrument also accompanied ritual song and dance, and it survived among folk musicians into the 19th century, when it was revived for concert and ethnographic performance.
source: Novgorod archaeological finds; byliny of Sadko

name: Samovar (Russian Tea Urn)
description: Metal urn with a central fire-tube used to boil water for tea, a fixture of the Russian home from the early 18th century. The great workshops at Tula and in Moscow produced brass, nickel and silver samovars; around the samovar the family gathered for the evening tea, and it became a byword for hospitality in Russian daily life and literature. A charcoal fire burns in the inner tube, keeping the surrounding water at a rolling boil while the small teapot steeps on top, and the strong tea is poured from the spigot and diluted to taste in each cup. The form spread across Russia, Ukraine and the Caucasus and eastwards through Central Asia, and travellers carried samovars on long journeys. Tula became the centre of manufacture, and the city's museum of samovars preserves hundreds of examples, from the copper kettles of the 18th century to the mass-produced factory models of the 20th.
source: Tula State Museum of Samovars; Russian Museum of Decorative Arts

name: Balalaika (Russian Triangular Lute)
description: Three-stringed Russian lute with a characteristic triangular body, plucked or strummed to accompany folk songs and dances. The balalaika became a symbol of Russian folk music in the 19th century, when Vasily Andreyev standardised its sizes into a whole family of instruments; it is played solo and in orchestras, and its bright, percussive tone carries well in open-air music-making. The body is usually of spruce or maple, with three strings historically of gut and now of nylon or metal, and the left hand often uses a single downward stroke that produces the crisp, rhythmic drive of dance tunes. Andreyev's balalaika orchestra, founded in 1888, gave the instrument respectability and set off a craze for balalaika ensembles across Europe. It remains the best-known Russian folk instrument abroad, appearing in concert halls, films and comedy routines alike, and its solo repertoire is still taught in Russian music schools.
era: attested from the 17th century; standardised late 19th century
source: Russian folk music tradition; Andreyev's balalaika orchestra (1888)

name: Kokoshnik (Russian Women's Headdress)
description: Crest-shaped ceremonial headdress of Russian women, a stiff crown of brocade, velvet or silk embroidered with pearls, gold thread and beads. Worn over the braids from the 17th century, the kokoshnik varied by region, from horned and high-crested to flat-topped forms, and marked the married woman; after Peter the Great's court reforms it survived as festive wear in the provinces. The word derives from 'kokosh', the old Russian name for a hen or cockerel, from the crest-like shape, and the headdress was worn at weddings and church festivals together with the best dress. Regional types carry distinct names, such as the one-horned kika of Tula and the morshen of the north, each built on a stiffened cardboard or birch-bark base covered in rich fabric. Museums hold examples sewn with river pearls, and the form has been revived on the stage, in film and in neo-Russian fashion, making it one of the most recognisable images of Russian national costume.
material: brocade, velvet, silk, pearls, gold thread
source: Russian Ethnographic Museum; historic Russian dress studies

name: Rushnyk (Ukrainian Ritual Cloth)
description: Embroidered ritual cloth of Ukraine woven from linen or hemp and decorated with geometric and floral embroidery at both ends. The rushnyk hangs on icons, frames doors and windows, joins the couple's hands at weddings and lines the coffin at funerals; its patterns carry protective meaning, and a woman's rushnyk collection testified to her skill. Made on the home loom and embroidered with cotton or silk thread in red, black and white, the cloths are kept for decades and passed down through families as heirlooms. The name shares its root with 'ruka', the hand, for the towel used to wipe the hands, yet the ceremonial rushnyk is never used for ordinary washing. In the wedding the bride presents rushnyky to the groom's family, and the cloth laid under the couple's feet is kept as a talisman for the marriage. Ethnographic museums treat the rushnyk as a central emblem of Ukrainian material culture.
source: Ivan Honchar Museum; Ukrainian ethnographic collections

name: Pysanka (Ukrainian Decorated Egg)
description: Ukrainian Easter egg decorated by the wax-resist method: a stylus called pysachok draws lines of hot beeswax on the shell, which is then dyed in successive colours, ending with the wax melted away to reveal the pattern. Pysanky bear solar, plant and animal motifs linked to spring rebirth, and eggs were kept in the house as protective charms. The practice is ancient, and ornamented eggs from the region date back to pre-Christian times; the egg is sometimes said to carry the hope of the resurrection and the turning of the year. Each region keeps its own colours and motifs, from the black-red-white geometry of the Kyiv area to the floral wreaths of Podillia. Making pysanky is a seasonal craft concentrated in the days before Easter, and women guard their own family patterns. Today the craft is taught in schools and workshops and has spread around the world with the Ukrainian diaspora.
source: Ukrainian pysanka tradition; Lviv Ethnography Museum collections

name: Bandura (Ukrainian Zither-Lute)
description: Plucked string instrument of Ukraine combining a lute's neck with a zither-like soundboard holding up to several dozen strings, played by folk singers called bandurysts and kobzars. The kobzar tradition of singing epic dumy to the bandura is among Ukraine's most distinctive musical heritage; the instrument descends from the older kobza and spread across Ukraine from at least the 18th century. In performance the player fingers the melody on the neck while sweeping across the accompaniment strings on the soundboard, producing a resonant, harp-like texture. The blind kobzars who wandered the villages singing historical ballads were famed for long improvisations, and the term 'kobzar' became a byword for the wandering epic singer. The instrument survived the suppression of the kobzar guilds in the Soviet era and is now taught in conservatories, performed in ensembles, and honoured at festivals of Ukrainian music.
material: wood body, gut or metal strings
era: attested from at least the 18th century
source: Ukrainian bandura tradition; studies of the dumy epics

name: Polish Pisanki (Decorated Eggs)
description: Polish Easter eggs decorated by several regional techniques: batik wax-resist (pisanki), scratch-carving, and the solid raspberry-dyed eggs called byki. Patterns of rays, stars and plant sprigs vary by region, with Kraków, Łowicz and the Opoczno district known for distinct styles; eggs were exchanged at Easter as gifts and kept in the home as charms. The name comes from 'pisać', to write or paint, since the wax is drawn onto the shell with a pin dipped in a funnel of molten wax. The techniques include the kraszanki boiled in onion skins for a uniform red-brown, the skrobanki scratched through the dyed shell to reveal white, and the pisanki written with wax in several colours. In folk belief the decorated egg brought health and protection, and at Easter it was shared at the table and given to godchildren. The craft is still practised across Poland, and regions hold competitions in the days before Easter.
material: hen's egg, beeswax, dyes, scratching tools
source: National Ethnographic Museum, Warsaw; Polish ethnographic collections

name: Ciupaga (Podhale Axe-Staff)
description: Small axe with a long wooden haft carried by the highlanders (górale) of the Polish Tatra mountains as a walking staff, herding tool and dance prop. The ciupaga's haft is often carved, and highlanders strike it on the floor in the energetic zbójnicki dance; it accompanies the shepherd's life of the Podhale region and is a recognised emblem of Tatra highland culture. Its head resembles an ice-axe, with a short blade on one side and a rounded butt on the other, and it serves as a climbing stick, a lever, and a defence against wolves and bears. The wooden haft, up to a metre long, is a canvas for ornament: stars, suns and geometric bands are burned or incised into the ash or beech wood. The zbójnicki, the dance of the historic brigands who sheltered in the mountains, is performed with the ciupaga raised and struck, and the object remains a proud mark of highland identity worn on formal dress.
material: steel blade, ash or beech haft
source: Podhale highland culture studies; Tatra Museum, Zakopane
